title: Contingency Recovery of Missed Rotable Repair Warranties
one_liner: A success-fee auditor that finds repaired aircraft components that failed inside the shop's warranty window, and turns them into filed claims and cash.
customer: Small and mid-size operators with their own stores and a thin materials team. That means regional airlines, Part 135 cargo feeders and air-ambulance fleets, and Part 145 shops that buy their own exchange units. They pay 20-25% of whatever cash or credit is recovered, and nothing up front.
problem: A repaired starter-generator, bleed valve, hydraulic pump or fuel control that fails 4 months after the shop visit is often covered by warranty. Almost nobody claims it. The tech pulling the unit at 3 AM is trying to make a 6 AM departure and never sees the warranty terms. The repair invoice sits in accounts payable as a PDF. The removal record sits in the maintenance system, and hours and cycles sit in a third place. One materials coordinator owns thousands of removals a year, with 30-90 day claim windows. Three other leaks go unclaimed as well: 'no fault found' evaluation fees on units that were still under warranty, unreturned exchange cores that turn into penalty charges, and repair turnaround-time guarantees that shops never credit because nobody compares PO date to receipt date.
solution: Ingest three exports: removals and installs, PO and repair invoices (PDFs read with an LLM extractor), and the negotiated warranty terms. Match by part number and serial number, including interchangeable P/Ns. Flag every in-warranty failure, late repair turn, disputable NFF fee and open core. Then draft the claim on each vendor's own template, track it to a paid credit, and re-run monthly. Add a 3 AM 'is this unit under warranty?' lookup for maintenance control, so the claim gets started at the moment of removal.
why_now: Airline cost pressure on regionals is high, and mechanic wages rose sharply in 2024-2026, so labor cost per removal is up. Materials teams are being cut while fleets stay old. LLM invoice and PDF extraction only became reliable and cheap enough in the last 18 months, and that is the missing link, because the money sits in unstructured AP documents that MRO software never reads.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20-25% of recovered cash and credits, with a 12-month tail on the audit. Later add a $2-5k per month SaaS tier for continuous monitoring, and sell benchmark data on shop warranty behavior to airline procurement teams.
non_obvious_insight: The leak is not in the maintenance system, it is in accounts payable. The tech who removes the part, the coordinator who could file the claim and the department that paid the invoice never share a screen. MRO software vendors will not fix it because warranty terms live in negotiated PDFs, not fields. Repair shops know most eligible claims are never filed, and they price that into their rates. A contingency auditor is the same playbook as freight-audit and telecom-audit firms, aimed at a niche nobody has covered.
first_30_days: Pitch 10 directors of maintenance and materials managers at small regionals, cargo feeders and helicopter EMS operators. Offer a free 12-month leakage audit, and ask them for the three exports. Build the matcher in Python plus an LLM invoice parser, and use a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Deliver a ranked claim list to the first 2-3 customers, file the claims yourself, and sign the success-fee agreement on the first credit memo. Publish the aggregate audit finding, such as the percentage of eligible failures that were never claimed, as the lead magnet.

judge_notes: vc: rank 2/25 - Contingency audit with no upfront cost, proven freight-audit playbook, fast first cash; can expand to all capital-equipment warranties.
operator: rank 1/25 - Contingency, no budget needed, real leak, named buyer, known audit playbook, easy free-audit wedge and quick first credit memos.
contrarian: rank 6/25 - Contingency audit of unclaimed warranties buried in AP PDFs; no upfront cost, fast proof, LLM extraction just became viable.

competitors.name: Ramco Aviation (MRO/ERP software, warranty management module)
competitors.what_they_do: Full aircraft maintenance and materials ERP that lists 'Warranty Management' as a feature. Its FAQ claims customers 'achieve up to $6 million in savings on warranty claims'. The page names no customer, gives no detail on how vendor-repair warranty claims work, and I saw no contingency or done-for-you claim filing. This is the only competitor I could verify. It is software you run yourself, sold to large operators, not an outsourced success-fee auditor.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established enterprise vendor (part of Ramco Systems, listed in India). The claim is marketing copy and I could not verify it.

competition.white_space: Caveat: this verdict rests on thin evidence. The WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) after the first two lookups. Every further search was refused, and I did not work around that limit. I could only fetch vendor homepages directly. I found no dedicated contingency-fee warranty auditor for rotable repair claims. I also could not rule one out, because I could not run Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or 'startup + key terms' searches. Vendor pages I checked (Trax eMRO, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000, CAMP) showed no warranty-claims features on their homepages, but homepage silence is weak evidence. I could not check IFS Maintenix (HTTP 429). Gaps that look unserved: (1) an outsourced, success-fee service that reads unstructured repair-invoice PDFs and joins them to removal records. This is the cross-system join the idea describes. (2) Small and mid-size operators such as regionals, Part 135 fleets and air-ambulance operators, which sit below the large ERP buyers Ramco targets. (3) The adjacent leaks, meaning no-fault-found fees within warranty, unreturned core penalties and turnaround-time guarantee credits. None of the vendor pages I read mention these. Unverified risks from my own domain knowledge, not from research: power-by-the-hour and maintenance-service-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets. Shop warranty terms are often short and carry exclusions. Getting AP and maintenance-system exports from a small operator is hard. The addressable market may be small. Someone should check all of these before building.
competition.evidence_of_demand: Essentially none found. I could not run forum, RFP or regulation searches because the search budget was exhausted. The only indirect signal is Ramco's marketing claim of 'up to $6 million in savings on warranty claims' (https://www.ramco.com/aviation). It suggests warranty recovery is treated as a valued outcome. It is unattributed, so it is not proof that anyone pays for outsourced recovery. I found no evidence yet of operators paying contingency fees for this, of RFPs, or of forum complaints about unclaimed rotable warranties.
competition.kill_reason: n/a. Nothing found so far justifies a kill, but the research was incomplete. Re-run the existence check with a restored search budget before committing. Priority searches: 'aircraft component warranty recovery services', 'airline warranty audit contingency', Crunchbase/YC/Product Hunt for aviation warranty startups, and operator complaints about unclaimed repair warranties.
competition.sharper_angle: Start with a wedge that needs only the accounts-payable export, so you avoid the hardest data-access problem, which is integrating with each operator's maintenance system. Run a 'repeat-repair detector' on repair invoices. Flag any part number and serial number that comes back to the same shop within the warranty window, and flag no-fault-found evaluation fees, core-return penalties and late-turnaround credits on the same invoices. This works the way freight and telecom audit firms do: an AP file in, a claims list out, paid only on credits recovered. Sell it first to Part 145 shops and parts pools that buy many exchange units, and to lessors and asset managers who need warranty compliance across a portfolio. Regionals and EMS operators can come later. Add the maintenance-system removal data as a second phase to confirm failures the invoices alone cannot show. Position it as outsourced claim filing and vendor negotiation, which ERP warranty modules like Ramco's do not provide, and not as software.
